BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

output.page_summary: A table compares loose, dense, elastic and specialised connective tissues and adipose tissue by location and function. A classification tree divides plant tissues into meristematic and permanent tissues, with their further branches, and a plant sketch locates apical, intercalary and lateral meristems.

items.content: Types of Connective Tissues
items.type_note: A pure heading introduces the table.
items.exam_note: Introduces an important tissue comparison.

items.content: Types of Connective Tissues. Columns: Type of Tissue | Location | Function. Entries: Loose connective tissue; Dense connective tissue; Elastic connective tissue; Specialised connective tissue—(i) Cartilage, (ii) Bone, (iii) Vascular connective tissue (blood); Adipose tissue.
items.type_note: The visual table compares tissue types by location and function, so comparison is more specific than figure.
prerequisites: A tissue is a group of cells working together
items.exam_note: Tissue–location–function matching is important for objective questions.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Loose connective tissue | Location: Deep layers of skin, blood vessels, nerves and body organs. | Function: Support and elasticity.
items.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How does loose connective tissue compare with dense connective tissue in location and function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue is listed in deep skin layers, blood vessels, nerves and body organs and provides support and elasticity. Dense connective tissue occurs in tendons and ligaments and provides strong, compact binding.

teacher_understanding.question: What structural difference helps explain their different functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loose connective tissue has relatively loosely arranged fibres and more ground substance; dense connective tissue has closely packed fibres suited to resisting pulling forces.

teacher_understanding.question: How can loose connective tissue support organs while permitting movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its fibre network holds neighbouring structures together, while its less compact arrangement allows some movement and deformation.

items.exam_note: Remember the listed locations and the pairing of support with elasticity.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Dense connective tissue | Location: Tendons and ligaments | Function: Compactly pack structures to one another and provides great strength.
items.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do dense and elastic connective tissues compare in their listed roles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dense connective tissue in tendons and ligaments strongly binds structures together. Elastic connective tissue in lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords provides elasticity.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tendon generally connects muscle to bone, while a ligament generally connects bone to bone at a joint.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is dense connective tissue suitable for tendons and ligaments?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its closely packed collagen fibres provide tensile strength, helping these structures withstand forces transmitted by muscles and across joints.

items.exam_note: Tendons and ligaments are key examples; distinguish their attachments.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Elastic connective tissue | Location: Lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords. | Function: Provides elasticity
items.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do elastic and loose connective tissues compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both have elasticity among their listed functions. Elastic connective tissue is listed in lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords; loose connective tissue is listed in deep skin layers, blood vessels, nerves and body organs and also provides support.

teacher_understanding.question: How does elasticity differ from strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Elasticity is the ability to return towards the original shape after stretching. Strength is the ability to withstand force without failing.

teacher_understanding.question: How do elastic fibres help lungs and arteries?
teacher_understanding.answer: They permit stretching and recoil. This helps lung tissue return after expansion and arterial walls respond to pressure changes during the heartbeat.

items.exam_note: Learn all four locations, including trachea and vocal cords.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(i) Cartilage | Location: Ends of long bones, tip of nose, parts of larynx and trachea. | Function: Provides flexibility and support.
items.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How do cartilage and bone compare in this table?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cartilage occurs at long-bone ends, the nose tip and parts of the larynx and trachea, providing flexibility and support. Bone occurs in bones and provides protection, support and muscle attachment.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cartilage more flexible than bone?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cartilage has a firm but relatively flexible matrix. Bone has a mineralised matrix that makes it much more rigid.

teacher_understanding.question: How is cartilage useful at the ends of long bones?
teacher_understanding.answer: Articular cartilage provides a smooth surface that reduces friction and helps distribute loads as bones move at a joint.

items.exam_note: Cartilage locations and its flexibility distinguish it from bone.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(ii) Bone | Location: Bones | Function: Protection and support muscle attachment.
items.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the listed functions of bone differ from those of blood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone provides protection, support and muscle attachment. Blood transports oxygen and carbon dioxide and contributes to immune response and blood clotting.

teacher_understanding.question: How do bone and cartilage differ as supporting tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bone provides relatively rigid support because its matrix is mineralised; cartilage provides more flexible support.

teacher_understanding.question: How does muscle attachment to bone contribute to movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Muscles transmit pulling force to bones through tendons. Bones then act as levers around joints.

items.exam_note: Associate bone with protection, support and muscle attachment.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Specialised connective tissue—(iii) Vascular connective tissue (blood) | Location: Within blood vessels | Function: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide and immune response blood clotting.
items.type_note: This logical row compares a specialised tissue by location and function.

teacher_understanding.question: How does blood compare with bone and cartilage in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: All three appear under specialised connective tissue. Blood is within blood vessels and performs transport, immune response and clotting, whereas bone and cartilage have supporting roles.

teacher_understanding.question: How can blood be connective tissue despite being fluid?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells are suspended in an extracellular matrix called plasma. Connective tissues can have matrices with different physical properties, including a fluid matrix.

teacher_understanding.question: How are blood's listed functions distributed among its components?
teacher_understanding.answer: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; carbon dioxide travels in several forms, especially as bicarbonate in plasma. White blood cells support immune defence, while platelets and clotting proteins help stop bleeding.

prerequisites: Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma
items.exam_note: Blood is a specialised connective tissue; retain transport, immunity and clotting.

items.content: Type of Tissue: Adipose tissue | Location: Deep layers of skin, surrounding heart and kidneys and padding around joints. | Function: Support, protection, heat conservation and energy source.
items.type_note: This row supplies location and function criteria within a comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How do adipose and loose connective tissues compare in location and function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are listed in deep skin layers and both provide support. Adipose tissue is also listed around the heart and kidneys and as padding around joints; its additional functions are protection, heat conservation and serving as an energy source.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes adipose tissue from a mainly fibrous supporting tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Adipose tissue contains many fat-storing cells called adipocytes. This stored fat supports its energy-storage and insulation roles.

teacher_understanding.question: How does adipose tissue protect organs, conserve heat and supply energy?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fat deposits cushion structures, reduce heat loss beneath the skin and store lipids that can be broken down when the body needs energy.

items.exam_note: Remember its locations and all four functions.

items.content: Plant Tissues branches into Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue branches into Apical meristem, Intercalary meristem and Lateral meristem. Permanent tissue branches into Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue. Simple permanent tissue branches into Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma. Parenchyma branches into Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma. Sclerenchyma branches into Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids. Complex permanent tissue branches into Xylem and Phloem. Connecting lines and downward arrows show classification relationships, not a temporal sequence.
items.type_note: The diagram presents a hierarchy of tissue categories, so classification is more specific than figure.

teacher_understanding.question: Which are the main divisions and further branches of plant tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant tissues divide into meristematic and permanent tissues. Meristematic tissue includes apical, intercalary and lateral meristems. Permanent tissue includes simple and complex tissues. Simple tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; parenchyma includes aerenchyma and chlorenchyma, and sclerenchyma includes fibers and sclereids. Complex tissues include xylem and phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes the major categories in this tree?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue contains actively dividing cells involved in growth. Permanent tissues contain differentiated cells with specialised roles. Simple permanent tissues have one main cell type, whereas complex permanent tissues contain different cell types working together.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a student read the branching arrows?
teacher_understanding.answer: Follow a line from a parent category to its subcategories. For example, phloem belongs to complex permanent tissue, which belongs to permanent tissue, which belongs to plant tissues.

prerequisites: Parent categories and subcategories in a tree
items.exam_note: The full hierarchy supports classification, matching and odd-one-out questions.

items.content: Plant Tissues — root label; branches to Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue.
items.type_note: Names the root category of the classification tree.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two categories lie immediately below Plant Tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue and Permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What basic distinction separates these categories?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissues are regions of active cell division; permanent tissues consist of differentiated cells specialised for particular functions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a plant need both kinds?
teacher_understanding.answer: It needs new cells for growth and specialised cells for functions such as support, photosynthesis and transport.

items.exam_note: First division in the plant-tissue hierarchy.

items.content: Meristematic tissue — child of Plant Tissues; parent of Apical meristem, Intercalary meristem and Lateral meristem.
items.type_note: Names a category and its children in the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which meristems are shown under meristematic tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these three meristems differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: They differ by position: apical meristems occur at growing tips, intercalary meristems occur between mature tissue regions, and lateral meristems occur along the sides of stems and roots.

teacher_understanding.question: How do meristems contribute to growth?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their cells divide to produce new cells, which can enlarge and differentiate into tissues.

items.exam_note: Know the three positional meristem categories.

items.content: Apical meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
items.type_note: Names a leaf of the meristem classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue category contains apical meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does apical meristem differ from lateral meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical meristem occurs at root and shoot tips and contributes to length growth; lateral meristem occurs along the sides and contributes to increased girth.

teacher_understanding.question: How does activity at a tip increase plant length?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cell division produces new cells near the tip, and subsequent cell enlargement extends the root or shoot.

items.exam_note: Associate apical with tips and length growth.

items.content: Intercalary meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
items.type_note: Names a leaf of the meristem classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which group contains intercalary meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an intercalary meristem differ in position from an apical meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: An intercalary meristem occurs between mature tissue regions, often at the bases of internodes or leaves in grasses, rather than at the terminal growing tip.

teacher_understanding.question: How can intercalary meristems help grasses regrow after cutting?
teacher_understanding.answer: Basal dividing regions may remain after upper parts are removed and produce cells that support renewed elongation.

items.exam_note: Distinguish intercalary from apical and lateral meristems.

items.content: Lateral meristem — child of Meristematic tissue.
items.type_note: Names a leaf of the meristem classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains lateral meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lateral meristem differ from apical meristem in growth contribution?
teacher_understanding.answer: Lateral meristems contribute to increased thickness or girth, whereas apical meristems contribute to length growth.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a lateral meristem increase girth?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dividing cells in layers along the sides add new tissue, increasing the diameter of the stem or root.

items.exam_note: Associate lateral meristem with girth.

items.content: Permanent tissue — child of Plant Tissues; parent of Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue.
items.type_note: Names a category and its children in the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two groups lie under permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple permanent tissue and Complex permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do permanent and meristematic tissues differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Permanent tissue cells have differentiated for particular functions and generally do not actively divide; meristematic cells actively divide to produce new cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How do permanent tissues arise?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells produced by meristems enlarge and differentiate, acquiring structures suited to specialised functions.

items.exam_note: Know both subdivisions and their examples.

items.where_on_page: chart, below Permanent tissue on the left
items.content: Simple permanent tissue — child of Permanent tissue; parent of Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a category and its children in the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which simple permanent tissues are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Parenchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes simple from complex permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: A simple permanent tissue has one main kind of cell; a complex permanent tissue contains different kinds of cells working together.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does 'simple' not mean functionally unimportant?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes cellular composition. Simple tissues perform major roles such as storage, photosynthesis and support.

items.exam_note: Memorise the three members and distinguish them from xylem and phloem.

items.where_on_page: chart, below Permanent tissue on the right
items.content: Complex permanent tissue — child of Permanent tissue; parent of Xylem and Phloem.
items.type_note: Names a category and its children in the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which complex permanent tissues are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem and Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: How does complex tissue differ from simple tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex tissue combines different cell types in a common functional system; simple tissue is composed mainly of one cell type.

teacher_understanding.question: How do different cell types help a transport tissue work?
teacher_understanding.answer: Some cells form conducting pathways, while others provide support, storage or assistance to transport.

items.exam_note: Xylem and phloem belong to complex permanent tissue.

items.where_on_page: chart, left branch under Simple permanent tissue
items.content: Parenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue; parent of Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a simple tissue and its subtypes.

teacher_understanding.question: Which subtypes are linked to parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Aerenchyma and Chlorenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does parenchyma generally differ from sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Parenchyma generally consists of living cells with relatively thin primary walls. Mature sclerenchyma cells generally have thick, lignified walls and are dead.

teacher_understanding.question: How can parenchyma perform different functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its living cells may store materials, contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis or be arranged with large air spaces, producing functional specialisations.

items.exam_note: Know both named parenchyma subtypes.

items.where_on_page: chart, middle branch under Simple permanent tissue
items.content: Collenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue.
items.type_note: Names a member of the simple permanent tissue category.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains collenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does collenchyma differ from sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls and provides flexible support. Sclerenchyma generally has dead mature cells with thick, lignified walls and provides more rigid support.

teacher_understanding.question: How can collenchyma support a growing plant part?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its strengthened but relatively flexible walls resist mechanical stress while permitting growth and bending.

items.exam_note: Distinguish collenchyma from parenchyma and sclerenchyma.

items.where_on_page: chart, right branch under Simple permanent tissue
items.content: Sclerenchyma — child of Simple permanent tissue; parent of Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids.
items.type_note: Names a simple tissue and its subtypes.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two forms of sclerenchyma are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma fibers and Sclereids.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these forms differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres are typically long and narrow; sclereids are generally shorter and occur in varied shapes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is sclerenchyma suited to mechanical support?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its thick, lignified cell walls resist deformation and strengthen plant parts.

items.exam_note: Retain both sclerenchyma subtypes and their parent.

items.content: Aerenchyma — child of Parenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a subtype within the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue is the parent of aerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does aerenchyma differ from chlorenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Aerenchyma is characterised by large air spaces; chlorenchyma is characterised by chloroplast-containing cells suited to photosynthesis.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the air spaces help plants in aquatic or waterlogged conditions?
teacher_understanding.answer: They facilitate internal gas movement and can contribute to buoyancy in aquatic plant parts.

items.exam_note: Associate aerenchyma with parenchyma and air spaces.

items.content: Chlorenchyma — child of Parenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a subtype within the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which parent tissue contains chlorenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes chlorenchyma from aerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Chlorenchyma contains chloroplasts for photosynthesis, whereas aerenchyma has prominent air spaces.

teacher_understanding.question: How do chloroplasts enable chlorenchyma to make food?
teacher_understanding.answer: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll that captures light energy for photosynthesis, allowing cells to form carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water.

items.exam_note: Associate chlorenchyma with parenchyma and photosynthesis.

items.content: Sclerenchyma fibers — child of Sclerenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a subtype within the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue contains sclerenchyma fibers?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma, a simple permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do sclerenchyma fibers differ from sclereids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres are typically elongated and narrow, while sclereids are generally shorter and have varied shapes.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibres strengthen plant parts?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their elongated form and thick, lignified walls, often arranged in bundles, help resist pulling and bending forces.

items.exam_note: Preserve the book's label 'fibers' and its parent category.

items.content: Sclereids — child of Sclerenchyma.
items.type_note: Names a subtype within the classification.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue category contains sclereids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How do sclereids differ from sclerenchyma fibers?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclereids generally have shorter, varied shapes, whereas fibres are typically long and narrow.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can sclereids make plant parts hard or gritty?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their very thick, lignified walls form hard cells; such cells contribute to hard coverings and the gritty texture of pear flesh.

items.exam_note: Sclereids and fibers are sibling categories under sclerenchyma.

items.where_on_page: chart, left leaf below Complex permanent tissue
items.content: Xylem — child of Complex permanent tissue.
items.type_note: Names a member of the complex permanent tissue category.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does xylem differ functionally from phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem mainly transports water and dissolved minerals from roots towards aerial parts; phloem transports organic food from sources to regions that use or store it.

teacher_understanding.question: How is xylem suited to water transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its conducting elements form pathways for water, and their strengthened walls help resist collapse under the tension associated with transpiration.

items.exam_note: Classify xylem correctly and distinguish it from phloem.

items.where_on_page: chart, right leaf below Complex permanent tissue
items.content: Phloem — child of Complex permanent tissue.
items.type_note: Names a member of the complex permanent tissue category.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does phloem transport differ from xylem transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem carries organic food from sources to sinks, while xylem mainly carries water and minerals from roots towards aerial parts.

teacher_understanding.question: How can phloem transport serve both growing roots and developing fruits?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both can act as sinks that use or store sugars. Phloem connects food-producing or food-releasing sources with these sinks.

items.exam_note: Phloem is a complex permanent tissue, alongside xylem.

items.where_on_page: lower-left, beside and below the classification tree
items.content: A small upright shoot sketch shows a pointed growing tip, leaves at successive stem levels and highlighted growth regions. Apical meristem points to the shoot tip; Intercalary meristem points to a highlighted transverse region near a leaf base; Lateral meristem points to the longitudinal side region of the stem. The sketch locates meristems spatially rather than showing a sequence.
items.type_note: The sketch maps meristem positions on a plant, making structure more specific than figure.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the small shoot sketch show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows the positions of apical, intercalary and lateral meristems on a shoot.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the three meristems marked?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical meristem is at the shoot tip, intercalary meristem is at a transverse region near a leaf base, and lateral meristem is along the side of the stem.

teacher_understanding.question: How does their position relate to growth?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical and intercalary meristems contribute to elongation in their respective regions, while lateral meristems contribute to increased thickness.

items.exam_note: Useful for identifying meristems from position in a diagram.

items.where_on_page: shoot sketch, label to the right of the tip
items.content: Apical meristem — points to the growing tip of the shoot.
items.type_note: The label identifies a spatial growth region on the shoot.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the top label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical meristem.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does its pointer end?
teacher_understanding.answer: At the shoot's terminal growing tip.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this region help extend the shoot?
teacher_understanding.answer: It produces new cells by division; subsequent cell enlargement contributes to shoot elongation.

items.exam_note: Identify apical meristem by its terminal position.

items.where_on_page: shoot sketch, label on the left near an upper leaf base
items.content: Intercalary meristem — points to a highlighted transverse region of the shoot near a leaf base, below the terminal tip.
items.type_note: The label identifies a spatial growth region on the shoot.

teacher_understanding.question: What region does the side label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Intercalary meristem.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the intercalary region shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: As a transverse highlighted region near a leaf base, below the shoot tip.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an intercalary meristem produce local elongation?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dividing cells at the base of an internode or leaf produce new cells that enlarge, extending that region.

items.exam_note: Recognise a growth region between more mature plant regions.

items.where_on_page: shoot sketch, label below the stem
items.content: Lateral meristem — points to the longitudinal side region of the stem.
items.type_note: The label identifies a spatial growth region on the shoot.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the label beneath the shoot identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Lateral meristem.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is lateral meristem marked?
teacher_understanding.answer: Along a side region of the stem rather than at the tip.

teacher_understanding.question: How does division in this position affect the stem?
teacher_understanding.answer: It adds tissue along the sides and contributes to an increase in stem girth.

items.exam_note: Connect the lateral position with increased thickness.

notes.about: This review evaluates the extraction and teacher understanding for Page 8 of the 'Tissues and Its Types' unit, which contains an image-only table comparing connective tissues, a classification tree of plant tissues, and a diagram showing meristem locations.
key_questions: Are all rows and sub-entries of the 'Types of Connective Tissues' table accurately captured with their column headers?
Are all nodes and branches of the 'Plant Tissues' classification chart and the accompanying meristem shoot diagram captured?
Are the chosen content types (comparison, classification, structure) appropriate refinements of the proposed figure type, and do all items meet teacher-level depth?

decisions.decision: Accept the content-type overrides (comparison for table, classification for tree, structure for meristem sketch) instead of generic 'figure'.
decisions.reason: The maker provided clear type_notes, and these specific content types better reflect the pedagogical nature of the visual elements and enforce appropriate required questions.

decisions.decision: Flag the spelling normalized in item i25 ('Sclereids' vs 'Sclerides' on the image) as a minor issue.
decisions.reason: The chart prints 'Sclerides', which is a minor typo in the source diagram for standard 'Sclereids'; noting the exact print alongside the standard spelling is helpful but not blocking.

wrong.problem: The diagram image prints the label as 'Sclerides', whereas the item content normalizes it to 'Sclereids' without noting the source spelling.
wrong.fix: Record the exact visible label 'Sclerides (Sclereids)' or mention the source spelling in the content/notes.

checklist.note: All book facts and outside explanations are accurately distinguished and scientifically sound for UPSC/State PCS level.
The extraction is comprehensive and provides deep, mechanism-focused teacher Q&As for every table row and diagram node.
The maker's notes clearly state what the page is about, justify the main structural and typing decisions, and note punctuation/layout uncertainties in the table.
Nothing is truncated, summarized away, or left as 'etc.'.
Every visible heading, table row, classification node, and shoot diagram label has been captured as an item.
Only the running header ('Science and Technology') and page number ('94') are marked as boilerplate.
Every logical row of the connective tissues table (including the three sub-entries under Specialised connective tissue) appears as its own table_row item with all cells and column headers.
Both the plant tissue classification tree and the meristem shoot sketch have parent diagram items and individual diagram_label items capturing all branches, arrows, and pointers.
There are no mathematical equations or formulas on this page.
Each teachable item includes depth 1 and depth 2 questions that explain the underlying biological 'why' and 'how' rather than merely restating labels.
All answers are properly marked as 'book' or 'outside', and all outside biological explanations are accurate.
Using 'comparison' for the table, 'classification' for the taxonomy tree, and 'structure' for the anatomical shoot diagram accurately reflects the content and is well-justified in type_note.
Prerequisites are concrete, foundational biological concepts appropriate for the learners.
Exam importance ratings and notes are well-tailored to UPSC/State PCS objective questions.
Native text only had the header and page number; ambiguities in image punctuation were properly noted in 'uncertain'.
